Formal neuroradiology review of cervical MRI and CT with attention to compression direction and stenosis grade.
Basic systemic workup for weight loss: complete blood count, comprehensive metabolic panel, inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP), thyroid function, and age-appropriate cancer screening.

resident.chief_complaint: Progressive motor weakness and tingling sensation in both upper and lower extremities.
resident.history: Motor weakness initially manifested ten months prior and started in the lower extremities before involving the upper extremities. The patient also developed tingling sensation and numbness in both upper and lower extremities. Three months after symptom onset, she was evaluated at the neurosurgery department of another university for progressive motor weakness and tingling sensation. She was able to walk independently but with an observable mild wide-base gait. She reported weight loss of 10 kg during 2 months. CT and MRI showed OPLL at the level of C3-T1 and cervical spinal cord compression; on T2-weighted images, high signal intensity was seen in the cervical spinal cord at the C5-6 disc space level. Electrophysiological tests (NCS/EMG) were not performed at that time.
resident.physical_exam: Physical examination revealed mild motor weakness (Medical Research Council [MRC] grade 4+/5) in all extremities and mildly decreased tactile sensation in all extremities. Gait was independently ambulatory with an observable mild wide-base pattern. Reflex findings are not documented.

Mildly decreased tactile sensation in all extremities
Weight loss of 10 kg over 2 months
OPLL at C3-T1 with cervical spinal cord compression on CT/MRI
High T2 signal intensity in cervical spinal cord at C5-6 disc space level

resident.public_message: This patient presents with a ten-month history of progressive motor weakness that began in the lower extremities and progressed to involve the upper extremities, along with tingling and numbness in all four limbs. She reports a 10 kg weight loss over 2 months. Examination shows mild motor weakness (MRC 4+/5) and mildly decreased tactile sensation in all extremities, with a mild wide-based gait. CT and MRI demonstrate OPLL from C3 to T1 with cervical spinal cord compression and T2 hyperintensity at C5-6. Electrophysiological testing was not performed. Past medical history is not documented.

imaging.public_message: Reporting the case record's description only; the films were not available for review. CT and MRI reportedly showed OPLL from C3-T1 with cervical spinal cord compression. neurology.localization: Cervical spinal cord lesion (myelopathy), likely at C5-6 or multilevel due to C3-T1 OPLL. The pattern of progressive quadriparesis with sensory loss in all limbs and wide-based gait supports a cervical cord lesion, although upper motor neuron signs are not documented, so localization rests on an incomplete examination.

red_flags.finding: Weight loss of 10 kg over 2 months
red_flags.rationale: Unexplained by cervical cord compression; may indicate a systemic process (e.g., malignancy, metabolic) and warrants workup, but does not by itself provide an alternative explanation for the quadriparesis and sensory loss because the cord compression remains a plausible cause.
Absence of upper motor neuron signs (e.g., hyperreflexia, Babinski) prevents confirmation of myelopathy; this limits localization confidence but does not change the indication or plan.

Cannot exclude a coexisting peripheral neuropathy, which could contribute to symmetric weakness and sensory loss; this does not change current localization but should be considered if symptoms are atypical.

neurology.public_message: Localization is consistent with cervical myelopathy from C3-T1 OPLL, with T2 cord signal at C5-6. The clinical pattern—progressive quadriparesis with sensory loss in all limbs and wide-based gait—supports a cervical cord lesion, although upper motor neuron signs are not documented. Imaging-reported cord compression explains the dominant syndrome but not every finding. Red flags: (1) weight loss of 10 kg over 2 months—coexisting, unexplained by the cervical lesion and warrants systemic workup but does not currently offer an alternative cause; (2) reflex findings not documented—coexisting, limits confidence in myelopathic localization; (3) NCS/EMG not performed—coexisting, cannot exclude a peripheral neuropathy.

anesthesia.public_message: ASA grade II. Intraoperative MAP target 70 mmHg. Expected blood loss risk: moderate. Prone position tolerance: moderate. Extubation difficulty: unassessable because no airway assessment is documented. The record does not confirm systemic comorbidities; the 10 kg weight loss is unconfirmed and not used for grading.

preconditions_for_failure: Progressive worsening of motor strength or gait despite 3-6 months of structured conservative treatment
Development of new bowel or bladder dysfunction
Emergence of definitive upper motor neuron signs (e.g., hyperreflexia, spasticity, Babinski)
Radiographic progression of cord compression or T2 signal change on follow-up MRI
physiatrist_opening.public_message: This patient has mild myelopathy (MRC 4+/5, independent ambulation) from C3-T1 OPLL with T2 cord signal at C5-6. While progressive symptoms over 10 months and T2 signal change raise concern and argue against indefinite delay, a structured 3-6 month trial of conservative management remains a rational first step in the absence of clear upper motor neuron signs or rapid deterioration. Conservative care—including physical therapy, gait and balance training, posture modification, pain management, and close neurologic monitoring—has a reported success rate of about 50% for mild myelopathy, though outcomes are less predictable when cord signal change is present. I cannot overstate success beyond that. I strongly recommend completing the missing reflex examination and NCS/EMG before deciding surgery; weight loss also warrants systemic workup but does not preclude a conservative trial. Failure of conservative treatment should be declared only if any of my listed preconditions occur.

persuaded_by: The deputy director's argument that T2 hyperintensity at C5-6 indicates irreversible cord injury, combined with the documented 10-month progressive motor weakness, means a conservative trial would not reverse the myelomalacia and risks further cumulative neurologic deficit.
physiatrist_final.public_message: I have been moved by the argument that the T2 hyperintensity at C5-6 represents irreversible cord injury and the documented 10-month progression shows active disease; conservative therapy cannot reverse myelomalacia and waiting risks further deterioration. I therefore accept surgery as warranted, conditional on completion of the missing reflex examination and NCS/EMG, and a basic systemic workup for the weight loss. If those tests confirm cervical myelopathy and exclude a significant peripheral neuropathy, I agree with surgical decompression without mandating a 3-6 month conservative trial.

vice_opinions.assessment: This patient has progressive cervical myelopathy from extensive OPLL (C3-T1) with documented cord compression and T2 hyperintensity at C5-6. The ten-month progression of motor and sensory deficits, even if currently mild, in the presence of cord signal change indicates established myelopathy that is unlikely to stabilize with conservative care alone. The missing reflex examination, absent NCS/EMG, and unexplained weight loss require urgent investigation, but they do not justify a 3-6 month conservative trial when there is progressive cord compression. Surgical decompression should be planned after completing these evaluations.
proposed_options: Posterior cervical decompression and fusion (C3-T1 laminectomy or laminoplasty with instrumented fusion) after urgent completion of reflex examination, NCS/EMG, and systemic workup for weight loss.
Anterior cervical decompression and fusion if imaging confirms a focal anterior compressive lesion at C5-6 amenable to direct removal; less preferred with extensive C3-T1 OPLL.
Conservative management with physiotherapy and close monitoring for 3-6 months, only if surgery is deferred after complete workup and no progression; not my preferred option given cord signal change.
vice_opinions.preferred_option: Posterior cervical decompression and fusion (C3-T1 laminectomy or laminoplasty with instrumented fusion) after urgent completion of reflex examination, NCS/EMG, and systemic workup for weight loss.
disagreement_points: I disagree with the physiatrist's recommendation for a 3-6 month conservative trial as first-line; progressive myelopathic symptoms with T2 cord signal are an indication for surgery, not observation.

The lack of documented upper motor neuron signs does not exclude myelopathy; reflex findings must be obtained, but their absence should not delay a surgical decision when the myelopathic pattern is otherwise supported.

Weight loss of 10 kg over 2 months is concerning but likely a separate issue; it does not offer an alternative explanation for the cervical cord compression and should not block surgery if systemic workup is non-diagnostic.
deferred_questions_to_director: Should we proceed with surgical decompression immediately after urgent completion of NCS/EMG and reflex examination, or do you prefer to first complete systemic workup for weight loss?
Do you agree with a posterior approach, or would you consider anterior decompression if the compressive lesion is focal at C5-6?
Is there any circumstance under which you would endorse a conservative trial given the T2 signal change?
vice_opinions.public_message: Given the progressive myelopathy with cord signal change, I recommend proceeding with surgical decompression once the missing reflex examination and NCS/EMG are completed. A conservative trial is unlikely to reverse the cord injury and risks further deterioration.

director_rulings.final_decision: Proceed with surgical decompression and fusion for C3-T1 OPLL with progressive myelopathy and T2 cord signal at C5-6. Posterior approach is planned; anterior decompression will be considered if focused compression at C5-6 is confirmed on imaging review. Preoperative evaluation including reflex examination, NCS/EMG, and systemic workup for weight loss will be completed urgently but will not delay the surgical decision.
director_rulings.surgical_plan: Posterior cervical decompression and fusion (laminectomy or laminoplasty with instrumented fusion) from C3 to T1, with intraoperative neuromonitoring. Consider anterior approach if imaging review shows focal compression at C5-6 amenable to anterior decompression.
